content:
Currencies debased. 
Privacy under attack. 
Cash goes underground. 
The crushing weight of debt. 
We were never prepared. 

Welcome to a system designed to keep us poor. The harder we work, the less we gain.
And as we struggle, the noose only tightens. 
And then, when we have nothing left to lose, we turn on those who rigged the game. 
We stand and fight. 

These 21 stories portray unfortunate yet brilliant heroes fighting the powers that triggered financial fallout. Money is broken, but hope is not lost.

***

DM for access to access to a Underworld, a bonus story by Max Hillebrand.

Sara Jade is a keytar player and cinematic pop-rock songwriter. She built a following of more than 30,000 on Nostr, gets zapped in real time on TuneStr, and lives on a Bitcoin standard.
In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson sits down with Sara about leaving the old streaming economy. She tells the story of earning a million sats in a single acoustic set, from people in the room and people watching online. She explains why Spotify removed one of her singles for phantom streaming, and what it meant to open for Jason Mraz while stacking sats instead of streams.

Joe Martin is a singer-songwriter and a 21st century troubadour. The song comes first. He grew up in the UK, learned piano as a child, picked up his father's guitar as a teenager, and has spent a decade writing Americana and country, with trips to Nashville along the way. He is based on the Isle of Man. He is fully independent. He sells merch for sats.
In this episode, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson talks with Joe about Alone in Valentine, the album he made on purpose without AI. He recorded it in Nashville with Cal Campbell, son of Glen Campbell, and Cornelius Webb, son of Jimmy Webb. The title comes from Valentine, a town in West Texas, and he went there to shoot the artwork himself. It took nearly two years and most of his savings. He wanted a record that could outlive him.
He also tells the practical part. The first song he put on RSS made about $100 in a week, more than that song had made him on Spotify. A zap is the moment it clicks. Listeners are still catching up to the artists, and artists are still waiting for the listeners. His advice to a younger songwriter is plain: get on Nostr, put the music on RSS, and make it easy for someone to send sats. Save what arrives. That is low time preference. It means choosing the work that lasts over the post that has to perform this week.
Sound money is the other half. Inflation makes a real album more expensive while streaming pays less. AI makes a cheap song easy. Joe's answer is the human one. A machine has not lived the life the song comes from. People still want to stand in a room and hear it.

Fzero is a designer, illustrator, node runner, and co-founder of Ninefold, the studio he runs with Ivy Lumi. Their line is "stories that make you build." He started by copying manga as a kid. He studied economics, finance, and marketing, then opened stores and ran the floor for big fashion brands. The work looked like a career. It did not feel like one. On December 25, still under 30 and home with his family, he had a stroke. He already knew Bitcoin. He had been stacking sats for years. The scare settled the question. Time is the currency you cannot count, and he wanted to leave something that helps people after he is gone.
In this episode, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson talks with Fzero about the moment Bitcoin stopped being an idea and became a node in the house, about getting banned from X and staying on Nostr, and about pricing work once the payment is peer to peer. His GENESIS 113 pins are 21,000 sats. The shop is Take My Sats. He describes the first drawing that sent people to the Bitcoin white paper, the day a friend wore his alien as a tattoo at Nostriga, and GENESIS 113, the painting that treats Bitcoin as frequency: a tower of light rising out of noise. He made the painting. Timechain Art Magazine is featuring it in Edition One. It hung at The Space in Denver. The pins, made with Modeotec, went to BTC Prague and then to Plebeian Market.
He also tells the story of $BLEEP, the retro sci-fi series about an extraterrestrial trying to understand humanity through Bitcoin. The character is him, with the awkwardness left in. Season 1 is wrapped. Season 2 arrives in 2027. And he is plain about rooms and galleries. The artist creates first. Everyone else is there to serve the artist. The profit comes from serving them well.
This episode is on Fanfares this week. Your 21 sats go straight to Bitcoin For The Arts to fund artists. Next week the full video is free on YouTube.
IN THIS EPISODE: Drawing manga as a kid, then leaving it for economics and retail. Opening shops, running the floor, and feeling the art go missing. Tattooing as the way back. A skull, a dollar sign, and a QR code that opens the white paper. Why the details matter, and what gets lost when two people use the same word for different things. A European bank account that would not move the money. Running a node. The stroke on December 25. Time as the currency. COVID, cold storage, and who a stack is actually for. How a fiat job reaches the body, not just the bills. Joining Nostr and X in the same stretch, then losing the X account. Why Nostr stayed. Pricing pins at 21,000 sats. Take My Sats. Low time preference and the Mona Lisa on a donkey. Building in public. Why a middleman slows the work down. The alien tattoo at Nostriga, and the trust of drawing on skin. GENESIS 113: his painting, then Timechain Art Magazine Edition One, The Space in Denver, and a thank you to Asanoha. The Modeotec PCB pins, a run of 42, at BTC Prague and Plebeian Market. Who $BLEEP is for. Why a story teaches proof of work faster than a lecture. Kids' rooms in El Salvador and Las Vegas. Ninefold with Ivy Lumi, announced at Origin Seoul. Eight worlds, including $BLEEP, Life with Bitcoin, Zaza, and Tynka. Stories around the fire. What a gallery owes an artist. "What can I do for Bitcoin?" Season 2 of $BLEEP in 2027. What a $500 to $2,000 micro-grant would unlock.

Thomas Forsyth is a London designer, maker, and engineer. His work spans the Saatchi Gallery, Glastonbury Festival, the Wall Street Journal's Apple Car, and a Star Wars K-2SO build for Silicon Valley Comic Con. He calls himself a general handychap.
In this episode, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson talks with Thomas about why he uses that name, the three times Bitcoin showed up before it clicked, and why sound money and sound craft share a backbone.
Bitcoin crossed his path three times. First in a London bar around 2010. Then in 2018, while he was teaching himself about money. Then in 2024, when, as he puts it, it actually started doing what people said it would do.
His first Lightning payment was at a small Italian family restaurant in South London. "My thoughts became zaps and those zaps became food in your belly."
He also tells the 16-hour, mud-soaked Glastonbury story that taught him to work smart instead of long, talks about AI as one more tool from someone who lived through the second wave of 3D printing, and offers this to the next generation of makers: "I'd quite like to be around for a while, so I'll take things slow."
Your 2 sats go to Bitcoin For The Arts and help fund artists. This episode is also free on YouTube: https://youtu.be/ZepNitUDItg

Why he calls himself a general handychap. Work at the Saatchi Gallery, Glastonbury, the Wall Street Journal Apple Car, and a K-2SO build. Discovering Bitcoin three times before it clicked. The first Lightning payment, and zaps that became dinner. The Glastonbury lesson in low time preference. AI as another tool, from a maker who has seen tool waves before. Advice for working makers: take it slow.

Rami Korhonen has sung in the Finnish melodic punk band Fumble since the early nineties. One of their songs opens an episode of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit. A few years ago, on long business trips in the Middle East, he picked up a guitar he found in a rented apartment and started writing songs about Bitcoin, with one rule: the songs never say the word. He calls it acoustic pleb rock. The project is The Higher Low.
In this episode, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson sits down with Rami to trace the whole road: seeing the Ramones in Helsinki at sixteen, thirty years of DIY punk, recording twelve songs in one four-hour session over a Christmas break, the Bitcoin Beats invitation that turned them into the album Node To Freedom, and opening Bitcoin conference stages with one voice and one guitar.
He explains why his songs carry more than one meaning, what the name The Higher Low really means, the campfire test every song has to pass, and why he misses the freedom-tech spirit of Bitcoin's early culture. He tells the story of Knut Svanholm jumping on the drums at Baltic Honeybadger in Riga, writing Freedom Engine in El Zonte, handing his acoustic songs to Jesperi Mommo and the band for Freedom In the Digital Age, and crowdfunding the vinyl on Geyser.
His sats from music are never spent. "One day it's going to be enough to do another album."
This episode is a one-week Fanfares exclusive. Your 21 sats go straight to Bitcoin For The Arts to fund artists. Next week it goes free on YouTube and RSS.
IN THIS EPISODE:
Seeing the Ramones at sixteen and starting Fumble. Walk Alone in 1992, the break, and the 2006 comeback. The Law & Order: SVU song. Two people and a dog: playing every show like a festival. A guitar in a rented apartment and writing LFG on the spot. Twelve songs in one four-hour session. Bitcoin Beats, Boston, and Node To Freedom. Why the songs never say Bitcoin. What a higher low really means. Finding Bitcoin in 2017 and The Bitcoin Standard in 2020. The music pyramid, the fiat pyramid, and value for value. The campfire test. One guitar, nothing to hide behind. Opening the room at Bitcoin conferences. Knut Svanholm on drums in Riga. Freedom Engine in El Zonte. Handing the songs to the band. BTChel launch and the Geyser vinyl. Saving every sat for the next album. The next five years. What a $500 to $2,000 micro-grant would unlock.

Classically trained in London, disillusioned in Reykjavik, now in the mountains of central Italy with his family, Anik Malcolm makes some of the most rigorous fine art in the Bitcoin space. Tagline: Depicting Bitcoin. Main work: The Whole Entire Universe, debuted at Bitcoin 2026 in Las Vegas after 900+ hours. Twenty-one million beads. Cube of 276 by 276 by 276. Each face 4,096 squares. The halving pattern lives in the image, and it only works cleanly at 21 million.

Dion talks with Anik from childhood making, to London training, to the gallery moment that broke the spell, to Italy, to Bitcoin becoming the whole practice, to Lugano and Roatan outside the museum circuit, to fatherhood, to what craft looks like outside MoMA.

This Fanfares edition uses the YouTube version audio with intro clips and the closing animation walkthrough. The RSS audio does not have the intro.

Philip lives in Gran Canaria. He is the co-editor of 21 Futures: Tales from the Timechain, a collection of twenty-one stories from twenty-one authors including Knut Svanholm and Ioni Appelberg, released by Konsensus Network in 2023 and presented at Bitcoin Atlantis in 2024. In this conversation, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson sits down with Alana Mediavilla, the Puerto Rican filmmaker behind the award-winning documentary Dirty Coin and founder of Campo Libre in San Juan.
Alana spent more than a decade inside Silicon Valley producing for Google, Apple, PayPal, Volkswagen, and Volvo, including four years as a video producer for Google Cloud. In 2020 she walked away, moved her family home to Puerto Rico, and built the most important documentary on Bitcoin mining ever made. Dirty Coin has since been screened in over 200 cities through a community-hosted distribution model and won Best National Documentary in Puerto Rico, the first English-language film ever to do so.
This is the full story: a photographer father at Kodak, a Cuban mother whose family left Havana under Fidel, the personal sovereignty question that runs through every choice she has made since, and why the next decade of cinema belongs to artists who control their own rails.

Mississippi mother Lindey Magee never planned to become a Bitcoin author. In August 2024, her husband Chuck lost his battle with cancer after twenty-five years of marriage, leaving her a widow with two children and no traditional income. Twelve years earlier, her then-twelve-year-old son Bennett had tried to teach her about Bitcoin. In grief, that conversation came back.

In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson sits down with Lindey Magee, author of the Seuss-style rhyming children's book Bitcoin: A Treasure to HODL, which debuted at Bitcoin 2025 in Las Vegas and is now in the Ingram catalog for nationwide bookstore, library, and school distribution.

Lindey walks through her journey from grieving widow to Bitcoin advocate. She talks about the Holy Spirit conviction that led her to put Chuck's life insurance into Bitcoin, the New Year's Eve she sat down at her kitchen table and wrote most of the book by three in the morning, the offset print run of ten thousand copies she committed to on her own, and the thirty thousand dollars she has invested in the book while raising her teenage daughter on a Bitcoin standard, currently from inside a twenty-six foot Winnebago after mold destroyed their home.

On August 8, 2022, the United States Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Tornado Cash, a decentralized smart contract protocol on Ethereum.

Within hours, GitHub suspended the accounts of the core developers, deleted their code repositories, and revoked access to years of open-source documentation. Simultaneously, centralized RPC node providers like Infura and Alchemy blocked user requests interacting with the protocol addresses.

This event sent shockwaves across the software development community. It exposed a critical vulnerability in modern open-source development: **The code itself may be decentralized, but the tools, repositories, and communications used to build it remain deeply centralized.**

If a handful of corporate infrastructure providers can delete code repositories, revoke developer identities, or silence discussions at the request of state actors, then the software stack of the modern web is built on sand.

Building true censorship resistance requires more than just decentralized money or permissionless social feeds. It requires **decentralized, uncensorable developer tools**.

When newcomers first enter the Bitcoin ecosystem, they often carry a common misconception: they believe Bitcoin is completely anonymous.

In reality, the base layer of Bitcoin operates on a transparent, public ledger. Every transaction, wallet balance, and UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) is broadcast to tens of thousands of nodes worldwide.

In an era where blockchain surveillance firms and regulatory authorities maintain massive databases linking public addresses to real-world identities (via Exchange KYC protocols), maintaining financial privacy has become a major operational challenge.

If every coffee purchase or article donation you make on-chain can be traced back to your primary savings stack, your financial sovereignty is compromised.

Privacy is not about hiding illegal activity; **privacy is the fundamental right to selectively reveal yourself to the world.**

This guide breaks down the essential tools and habits needed to obscure your digital footprint on the Bitcoin base layer and the Lightning Network, ensuring your financial life remains strictly private.

Central banks around the world are facing a historic dilemma. Physical cash—the last remaining mechanism for private, anonymous, and permissionless transaction—is rapidly disappearing from daily commerce. In its place, payment processing giants and commercial banks have constructed a digital surveillance dragnet that logs every coffee purchase, peer-to-peer transfer, and monthly subscription.

To solidify their control over the future of value, over 100 central banks are currently developing Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs).

Promoted under the banner of modern efficiency and financial inclusion, CBDCs are framed as the natural evolution of cash. But behind the glossy marketing lies a fundamental shift in the nature of money itself.

A CBDC is not simply digital paper money. It is programmable credit. It grants central planners the technical ability to implement negative interest rates, attach expiration dates to your savings, restrict purchases based on carbon quotas, or instantly freeze funds without due process.

> *"When money becomes programmable by central authorities, spending is no longer an economic decision—it becomes a conditional permission."*

The push for total financial control is setting up the ultimate battle for the future of trade. On one side stands centralized financial surveillance; on the other stands the unshakeable architecture of open protocols.

For decades, the Cypherpunk movement remained a niche subculture of mathematicians, hackers, and privacy advocates. But today, in 2026, those theoretical concepts have transformed into global, censorship-resistant infrastructure.

# Julian Assange Is Back: What 20 Years of Censorship Resistance Taught Us

On September 17, 2026, a two-word message appeared on Julian Assange’s X account:

**“I’m back.”**

It was enough to immediately capture global attention.

The post marked his first personal message in over two years, following a silence that began on June 28, 2024, shortly after the legal agreement that ended his long-running prosecution in the United States.

The official WikiLeaks account confirmed the return with a photograph and a concise message: *“He’s back @JulianAssange.”* His wife, Stella Assange, added that further news would follow in the coming week.

For millions seeing his name headline the news today, one fundamental question arises: **Who exactly is Julian Assange, and why do two words from him shake the global digital landscape?**

To understand the weight of his return, we have to look back over two decades of political warfare, investigative journalism, and the rise of censorship-resistant technologies.

> *"If journalism is good, it is controversial by nature."*
>
> — **Julian Assange**

# What is a vacation anyway?

Especially when it seems like every day is a new nail in the 'the world is ending, economic winter is upon us, enter the bunkers!'

Well, for two weirdos in September of 2026 a 'vacation' meant...

Gallavanting around São Paulo, visiting family and friends while grappling with various mid life crises.

## The weirdos:

M: A native Brazilian, youngest of 7, who moved to the USA after hooking up with a scientist. Likes the color green, maybe the most level headed of the herd, crippled by shoulder centered nerve issues. 

Jr: An emo who follows M around for lack of anything better to do. Raised in the US, crippled by financial anxieties and a lack of any familial roots or support system. Brought too much misc crap, stained pants with mustard. 

# Why? 

Around July, M noticed that nothing in life was going as planned. Work was in a weird inbetween due to two factories consolidating,  resulting in a tense environment covered in a fog of layoffs and incoming machines + personnel. House hunting plans were going stale in a market of high bidding buyers, economic doomerism(from Jr), and an uncertain retirement looming... After talking to one of her 'go getter' nieces, she found herself having made a payment on a sitio rental, and with plane tickets purchased. Life lesson: "The stars will never align, so get up and do what has to be done." 

A very true but very unfortunate life lesson... husbands don't fall from the sky, art skills don't manifest themselves, and the perfect steak never gets made if you let it rot in the fridge... 

Jr's contribution: $$ and a warm body 👌

## Criteria for a successful trip: 

No fatalities 

Lots of hugs with family

Pet lots of dogs (Jr)

## The Itinerary:

Landed in Guarulhos, SP

Drove 3 hours to São Carlos for a 5 day stay with M's hubby(the scientist), S. 

Drove back to the Casa Verde region, stayed with S's fam and visited some of M's family and friends via Metro / Train / Uber

Drove down through Fog and mountains (" The Serra") to Bertioga and stayed with M's fam

Main event, a 2 day stay in a rented Sitio in the Mogi das Cruzes region for a family reunion

Last day, back in Casa Verde before the plane flight. 

A vacation back to your home country is for sure different than somewhere you've never been. Tbh I can't say either one of us is less stressed than before, but maintaining connections to family and friends is worth it. 

# WHAT KIND OF TRIP THIS WAS

Not Tourism: ... we went to the Ecological Park of Sao Carlos (a Zoo)- We also went to the Bi-Annual Book Festival in São Paulo! \
All about Family: a little bit in each area, all doing their own thing to survive. \
Heritage: uhh... \
Everyday life: is all about working hard to grasp opportunities and find the bright spots in a dreary world.\
What we deliberately did differently from a normal vacation: bro idk what a normal vacation even is... the last time I relaxed during a vacation was when I didn't know what taxes were ;w;

# WHAT THIS SERIES WILL EXPLORE

Money: I mean we prolly spent less than 'tourists', but not nothing... \
Food: We ate a lot. I bet you'll be surprised by the meaning of a traditional brazilian hotdog! \
Family: Always manage to f up your plans!\
Culture: Hugs and Kisses for everyone! Technically it's supposed to be a brief hug with an air kiss to the cheek. Jr doesn't understand this custom, and kisses everyone indiscriminately! Those who are too tall get kissed on the neck... \
Transportation: Car, Metro, Train, and Uber!\
Language: Portuguese!\
Unexpected experiences: A stray dog decided to hang out with us during the family reunion. We messed up during check in for the flight to Brazil by using the wrong passports... My cards didn't work and I nearly cried, multiple times!! 

Below, I'll attach some pictures from throughout the trip as a thanks if you send some zaps, but no pressure. 

I'll be writing more about each part of the trip soon. See ya!
